items.title: How to Have Enough: Wendell Berry on Creativity and Love
items.description: “Enough is so vast a sweetness, I suppose it never occurs, only pathetic counterfeits,” Emily Dickinson sighed in one of her love letters to Susan an epoch before Kurt Vonnegut, in a short and lovely poem, distilled happiness to the knowledge that you have enough. items.title: A Parliament of Owls and a Murder of Crows: How a Forgotten Medieval Woman Gave Groups of Birds Their Strange Names, with Wondrous Vintage Illustrations by Brian Wildsmith
items.description: Language is an instrument of great precision and poignancy — our best tool for telling each other what the world is and what we are, for conveying the blueness of blue and the wonder of being alive. But it is also a thing of great pliancy and creativity — a living reminder that how we name things changes what we see, changes the seer. (This, of course, is why we have poetry.) items.title: How Do We Know What We Want: Milan Kundera on the Central Ambivalences of Life and Love
items.description: "We can never know what to want, because, living only one life, we can neither compare it with our previous lives nor perfect it in our lives to come... We live everything as it comes, without warning."

items.title: Wendell Berry on Solitude and the Two Great Enemies of Creative Work
items.description: "True solitude is found in the wild places, where one is without human obligation. One’s inner voices become audible... In consequence, one responds more clearly to other lives."

items.title: The Paradox of Knowing Who You Are and What You Want: Cristina Campo on Fairy Tales, Time, and the Meaning of Maturity
items.description: “If you want your children to be intelligent, read them fairy tales,” Einstein reportedly told one mother who wished for her son to become a scientist. “If you want them to be very intelligent, read them more fairy tales.” Given that the deepest measure of intelligence is a plasticity of being that allows us to navigate uncertainty, given that uncertainty is the pulse-beat of our lives, fairy tales are not — as J.R.R. items.title: The Invention of Zero: How Ancient Mesopotamia Created the Mathematical Concept of Nought and Ancient India Gave It Symbolic Form
items.description: "If you look at zero you see nothing; but look through it and you will see the world."

items.title: The Power of Being a Threshold Person: Liminality, Communitas, and the Anti-structures of Possibility
items.description: “All things are so very uncertain, and that’s exactly what makes me feel reassured,” one of the Moomins observes in Tove Jansson’s masterwork of philosophy disguised as a children’s book. It takes a great spaciousness and sobriety of spirit to be vitalized rather than paralyzed by uncertainty. items.title: A Lei for Your Losses: Joan Didion on the Art of Letting Go
items.description: “We cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss,” Judith Viorst wrote in her defense of life’s necessary losses, “and we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and leaving and letting go.” We know that loving anything or anyone is a contract with loss, and yet we love anyway, our lives a ceaseless osmosis of holding on and letting go, an endless apprenticeship in the art of losing. items.title: The Art of Choosing Love Over Not-Love: Rumi’s Antidote to Our Human Tragedy
items.description: "You’ll long for me when I’m gone... You'll kiss the headstone of my grave... Kiss my face instead!"

items.title: The Creative Power of Uncertainty: Polish Poet Wisława Szymborska’s Magnificent Nobel Prize Acceptance Speech
items.description: "Whatever inspiration is, it's born from a continuous ‘I don't know.’"

items.title: Italo Calvino on Reading and Sex
items.description: "Lovers’ reading of each other’s bodies... differs from the reading of written pages in that it is not linear... What makes lovemaking and reading resemble each other most is that within both of them times and spaces open, different from measurable time and space."

items.title: Wendell Berry on Hope, Despair, and the Measure of Effective Protest
items.description: The current of life is charged by the poles of hope and despair. What we make of our hopes and their devastation may be the purest measure of who we are and what we leave behind. Protest is what we call the resistance we launch against our reasons for despair — personal, political, existential. items.title: Everything Is Already There: Javier Marías on the Courage to Heed Your Intuitions
items.description: "This has nothing to do with premonitions, there is nothing supernatural or mysterious about it, what’s mysterious is that we pay no heed to it."

items.title: The Thing Itself: C.S. Lewis on What We Long for in Our Existential Longing
items.description: "...only the scent of a flower we have not found, the echo of a tune we have not heard, news from a country we have never visited."

items.title: The 3 Buddhist Steps to Repairing a Relationship
items.description: "The intention of deep listening and loving speech is to restore communication, because once communication is restored, everything is possible."
